# Match, deduplicate and link records {#sec-uc-link}

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
source("_setup.R")
source("_people.R")
```

Record linkage -- finding the records that refer to the same person,
business or address, within one file or across several -- has the same
shape whatever the data:

1. **Standardise** the fields you compare (@sec-uc-clean).
2. **Generate candidate pairs** cheaply, so that only plausible pairs are
   compared in detail: blocking, the sorted neighbourhood method, or a
   similarity search.
3. **Score** each candidate pair, field by field.
4. **Decide** which pairs are matches.
5. **Cluster** the matched pairs into entities.

[`rLink()`](#sec-rlink-link) does steps 2 and 3 in one call. The rest of
this chapter is the toolbox underneath it, for the cases where you want to
drive each stage yourself. @sec-workflow takes a messy pair of files all
the way through, including the standardising and the decision.

For `rLink()` itself --- worked from the simplest useful call up to a
staged production linkage of people, field by field --- see @sec-rlink,
and @sec-rlink-inspect for reviewing the pairs it cannot settle.

| Stage | Functions |
|---|---|
| Blocking **and** scoring in one call | `rLink()` |
| Candidate pairs from keys | `block_pairs()`, `sorted_neighbourhood()` |
| Phonetic keys | `soundex()`, `nysiis()`, `metaphone()`, `double_metaphone()`, `daitch_mokotoff()`, `statcan()`, `phonex()`, `onca()`, `caverphone()`, ... |
| Candidates by similarity search | `fuzzy_within()`, `tfidf_top_n()`, `tfidf_match()`, `minhash_pairs()`, `fuzzy_top_n()` |
| Scoring | `jaro_winkler()`, `jaro_winkler_tokens()`, `editex()`, `monge_elkan()`, `smith_waterman()`, `lcs_str()`, `levenshtein()`, `fuzz_*()` |
| Explaining a score | `edit_ops()` |
| Entities from matches | `cluster_pairs()` |

## Two files of people {#sec-uc-link-data}

Everything below works on the same pair of files: an enrolment extract and
a claims extract that hold the same people, recorded by two systems that
agree about nothing except who those people are. `docs/_people.R` in the
repository builds them, with a `person_id` kept aside so every claim in
this chapter can be checked rather than asserted.

```{r}
#| label: data
files <- people_files(n_enrol = 20000, overlap = 0.6)
enrol  <- files$enrol
claims <- files$claims

str(enrol[1:3, c("enrol_id", "given_name", "surname", "dob", "sex",
                 "number", "street", "street_type", "suburb", "postcode")],
    vec.len = 2)
claims[1:4, ]
```

The claims file is the awkward one, and awkward in all the usual ways: the
whole name in one `"SURNAME, Title Given Middle"` field in title case with
doubled and trailing spaces, the date of birth as `"DD/MM/YYYY"` text, sex
spelled out (and sometimes blank), the address as one line with
abbreviated street types and a unit prefix, and a *numeric* postcode, so
`0823` arrived as `823`.

@sec-workflow standardises it field by field. For now, here it is in one
block, so that the examples below have two files with the same column
names and the same types:

```{r}
#| label: standardise
titles        <- c("MR", "MRS", "MS", "MISS", "DR", "PROF")
street_abbrev <- c("ST", "RD", "AVE", "CT", "PL", "TCE", "PDE", "CRES", "DR", "LN")
street_full   <- c("STREET", "ROAD", "AVENUE", "COURT", "PLACE", "TERRACE",
                   "PARADE", "CRESCENT", "DRIVE", "LANE")

name <- fsquish(fupper(claims$patient_name))                  # one pass, no case left
rest <- fsquish(freplace_tokens(ftrimws(fsplit_field(name, ",", 2)),
                                titles, rep("", length(titles))))
addr <- fgsub("^U[0-9]+/", "", fupper(claims$address_line))   # drop the unit prefix

claims_std <- data.frame(
    claim_id       = claims$claim_id,
    given_name     = fsplit_field(rest, " ", 1),
    middle_name    = fsplit_field(rest, " ", 2),
    surname        = ftrimws(fsplit_field(name, ",", 1)),
    dob            = fas.Date(claims$date_of_birth, format = "dmy"),
    sex            = c(Male = "M", Female = "F", Unknown = "U")[claims$gender],
    street_address = fsquish(freplace_tokens(ftrimws(fsplit_field(addr, ",", 1)),
                                             street_abbrev, street_full)),
    suburb         = ftrimws(fgsub(" VIC$", "", fsplit_field(addr, ",", 2))),
    postcode       = fpad(as.character(claims$postcode), 4, pad = "0"),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
claims_std$sex[is.na(claims_std$sex)] <- "U"

# The enrolment file keeps its address in parts; join them the same way.
enrol$street_address <- fsquish(paste(enrol$number, enrol$street,
                                      enrol$street_type))
head(claims_std, 4)
```

## Blocking and scoring in one call: `rLink()` {#sec-rlink-link}

`rLink()` takes the two data frames, a list of blocking *passes*, and a
list of comparators, and returns one row per candidate pair with the
compared columns side by side and a score column for each comparator.
Blocking keys and comparison fields are written as ordinary R expressions
evaluated against the data, so a phonetic code or a date part goes in the
call rather than into a column prepared beforehand:

```{r}
#| label: rlink
cand <- rLink(
    enrol, claims_std,
    block = list(
        surname_dob  = list(soundex(surname), dob),
        surname_year = list(soundex(surname), format_date(dob, "y")),
        given_dob    = list(soundex(given_name), dob),
        name_postcode = list(soundex(surname), fsubstr(given_name, 1, 1), postcode)
    ),
    compare = list(
        surname  = jaro_winkler(surname),
        given    = jaro_winkler_tokens(given_name),
        dob      = (function(a, b) a == b)(dob),
        sex      = (function(a, b) a == b | a == "U" | b == "U")(sex),
        address  = jaro_winkler_tokens(street_address),
        suburb   = jaro_winkler(suburb),
        postcode = (function(a, b) a == b)(postcode)
    ),
    keep = c("enrol_id", "claim_id", "surname", "given_name", "dob", "sex",
             "street_address", "postcode")
)
dim(cand)
cand[1:3, 1:12]
```

The outer `list()` separates passes; a pair is a candidate if it agrees on
*any* one pass, each pair is reported once, and `pass` records the first
pass that found it. Inside a pass, `list()` joins terms into one key, so
`list(soundex(surname), dob)` requires the same surname code **and** the
same date of birth. A comparator's first argument names the column to
compare; anything else is its own options. Any function of two character
vectors works, which is how `sex` and the exact `dob`/`postcode`
comparisons above are written inline.

Three things are worth knowing straight away.

**Scores are oriented for you.** Comparators disagree about which end of
their scale means "identical": `jaro_winkler()` returns 1, `levenshtein()`
returns 0, the RapidFuzz `fuzz_*()` scorers return 100. `rLink()` probes
each one on a calibration pair and converts, so **1 always means an exact
match**. What it found is recorded, and is worth reading once:

```{r}
#| label: rlink-compare
attr(cand, "compare")
```

**Comparators see text.** Every comparison column is converted to
character first, so a `Date` reaches the comparator as `"YYYY-MM-DD"`.
Exact agreement therefore just works, but a *tolerance* needs the date
back:

```{r}
#| label: rlink-dob-near
near_dob <- function(a, b, days = 1)
    abs(as.numeric(fas.Date(a)) - as.numeric(fas.Date(b))) <= days
head(rLink(enrol, claims_std,
           block = list(list(soundex(surname), postcode)),
           compare = list(dob_within_1 = near_dob(dob)),
           keep = c("surname", "dob"))[, -1], 4)
```

**Where the time goes is on the object.** `attr(cand, "timings")` breaks
the call into stages, which is how you find the pass that is about to
explode:

```{r}
#| label: rlink-timings
attr(cand, "timings")
```

### Read the pass table before you trust the design

Because `pass` records the pass that found each pair, and because these
files come with a known truth, each pass can be audited for what it
actually contributed:

```{r}
#| label: pass-audit
truth <- same_person(files, cand$index_1, cand$index_2)
cbind(candidates = table(pass = cand$pass),
      true_pairs = tapply(truth, cand$pass, sum),
      yield      = round(tapply(truth, cand$pass, mean), 3))

c(true_pairs_in_data = true_pair_count(files),
  found_by_blocking  = sum(truth),
  pairs_compared     = nrow(cand),
  pairs_possible     = as.numeric(nrow(enrol)) * nrow(claims_std))
```

Blocking found every true pair in the data while comparing
`r format(nrow(cand), big.mark = ",")` of the
`r format(as.numeric(nrow(enrol)) * nrow(claims_std), big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE)`
possible ones. The pass table also shows what each pass costs: pass 2
(surname code plus year of birth) generates most of the candidates for a
few hundred extra matches. It is the pass that survives a transposed day
and month, so it earns its place -- but it is the one to tighten first if
the run gets too big, with `max_block_size` or a narrower key.

### Deciding, and clustering

Combine the score columns however your project justifies -- hand weights
here, a Fellegi-Sunter model in `fastLink` or `reclin2` on real data -- and
look at the two distributions before picking a threshold:

```{r}
#| label: decide
cand$score <- with(cand,
    (3 * surname + 2 * given + 2 * dob + 0.5 * sex +
     address + suburb + postcode) / 10.5)

qs <- c(0.01, 0.05, 0.5, 0.95)
round(rbind(same_person = quantile(cand$score[truth], qs),
            different   = quantile(cand$score[!truth], qs)), 3)
```

The two are well separated: the weakest 1% of true pairs still score above
the strongest 5% of false ones, so a threshold anywhere in the gap is
defensible.

```{r}
#| label: threshold-sweep
for (t in c(0.70, 0.75, 0.78, 0.82, 0.85)) {
    keep <- cand$score >= t
    cat(sprintf("%.2f  links %6s  precision %.4f  recall %.4f\n", t,
                format(sum(keep), big.mark = ","), mean(truth[keep]),
                sum(truth & keep) / true_pair_count(files)))
}
```

Then turn the accepted pairs into entity identifiers. `cluster_pairs()`
joins records connected by any chain of matches (the connected components
of the match graph); offset the second file's indices so the two files
share one numbering:

```{r}
#| label: cluster
links <- cand[cand$score >= 0.78, ]
entity <- cluster_pairs(links$index_1, links$index_2 + nrow(enrol),
                        n = nrow(enrol) + nrow(claims_std))
table(cluster_size = tabulate(entity))
```

Chaining is also the risk: if A and C do not match directly, their cluster
rests on B. Look at the largest clusters before trusting them, or raise
the threshold for pairs that would join two already-large clusters.

### Deduplicating one file

With one data frame, `rLink()` deduplicates it: pairs come back with
`index_1 < index_2` and no record paired with itself. Here the two files
arrive stacked, as a single extract, and the job is to find the people who
appear twice:

```{r}
#| label: dedupe
shared <- c("given_name", "surname", "dob", "sex", "street_address",
            "suburb", "postcode")
combined <- rbind(cbind(source = "enrol", enrol[, shared]),
                  cbind(source = "claims", claims_std[, shared]))

dup <- rLink(combined,
             block = list(list(soundex(surname), dob),
                          list(soundex(given_name), dob)),
             compare = list(given   = jaro_winkler_tokens(given_name),
                            surname = jaro_winkler(surname),
                            addr    = jaro_winkler_tokens(street_address)),
             keep = c("source", "surname", "given_name", "dob"))
nrow(dup)
dup[order(-dup$given - dup$surname), ][1:4,
    c("source_1", "source_2", "surname_1", "surname_2",
      "given_name_1", "given_name_2", "dob_1", "given", "surname")]
```

### Scoring pairs you found some other way

`pairs` takes candidate pairs from anywhere instead of blocking -- any data
frame with `x_index` and `y_index`, which is the shape
`minhash_pairs()`, `fuzzy_within()` and `tfidf_top_n()` all return:

```{r}
#| label: rlink-pairs-arg
candidates <- data.frame(x_index = c(1L, 2L, 3L), y_index = c(7L, 7L, 9L))
rLink(enrol, claims_std, pairs = candidates,
      compare = list(surname = jaro_winkler(surname)),
      keep = c("surname", "dob"))
```

### Columns named differently in the two files

`compare` takes `column_1 | column_2` when the two files call the same
thing by different names, and `block_2` gives the second file its own
blocking expressions, pass for pass:

```{r}
#| label: rlink-different-names
raw <- claims                       # the unstandardised claims file
raw$surname_raw <- ftrimws(fsplit_field(fsquish(fupper(raw$patient_name)), ",", 1))

head(rLink(enrol, raw,
           block   = list(soundex(surname)),
           block_2 = list(soundex(surname_raw)),
           compare = list(sn = jaro_winkler(surname | surname_raw)),
           keep    = c("surname", "surname_raw"))[, -1], 3)
```

## Candidate pairs by blocking, by hand

`block_pairs()` is the blocking engine `rLink()` calls, and is what to
reach for when you want the pairs without the scoring -- to count them
first, or to feed them somewhere else. It takes one column per pass:

```{r}
#| label: block-pairs
block_keys <- function(d) data.frame(
    surname_dob = paste(soundex(d$surname), d$dob),
    dob         = as.character(d$dob),
    initial_pc  = paste(fsubstr(d$given_name, 1, 1), d$postcode))

p <- block_pairs(block_keys(enrol), block_keys(claims_std))
nrow(p)
table(pass = p$pass)
```

A missing key (`NA`) never pairs with anything, which is what makes
blocking on an incomplete field safe: the records with no date of birth
simply do not appear in the passes that use it.

`max_block_size` skips blocks too big to be worth comparing -- the
commonest surname code, or the 1 January placeholder date -- and warns
with how many it dropped. How big a block gets is worth measuring before
you decide:

```{r}
#| label: block-sizes
sizes <- table(soundex(enrol$surname))
c(blocks = length(sizes), largest = max(sizes), over_400 = sum(sizes > 400))

# A surname-only pass, capped. A handful of codes go, and with them more
# than half the pairs the pass would have produced.
nrow(block_pairs(soundex(enrol$surname), soundex(claims_std$surname)))
nrow(block_pairs(soundex(enrol$surname), soundex(claims_std$surname),
                 max_block_size = 400))
```

## The sorted neighbourhood method

Exact keys miss pairs whose keys differ in the last characters (`SMITH`
and `SMITHE`). `sorted_neighbourhood()` sorts the distinct key values and
pairs records whose values are within `(window - 1) / 2` places of each
other, as well as records with equal values. A second pass on the
*reversed* key catches errors at the start of the string:

```{r}
#| label: sorted-neighbourhood
surname <- c("SMITH", "SMITHE", "SMYTH", "JONES", "JONSON", "XMITH")
p <- sorted_neighbourhood(data.frame(surname, freverse(surname)), window = 3)
data.frame(a = surname[p$x_index], b = surname[p$y_index], pass = p$pass)
```

`XMITH` only meets `SMITH` in the reversed pass. Note what else the window
pairs: `SMITH` with `JONSON`, because they are alphabetical neighbours, not
because they are alike. The method trades precision for recall by design,
so it belongs in a pass whose candidates are then scored, never on its
own. The window moves over distinct values, as in Python's `recordlinkage`
package, so the pairs do not depend on the order of the records and every
tie is paired. Keys can
be dates or numbers too: a date of birth with `window = 3` pairs dates one
day apart, which is exactly the transcription error that `format_date(dob,
"y")` above needed a whole extra pass to survive.

```{r}
#| label: sn-dates
d <- as.Date(c("1985-03-14", "1985-03-15", "1985-03-16", "1990-01-01"))
sorted_neighbourhood(d, window = 3)
```

`rLink(block_method = "sorted_neighbourhood", window = 3)` uses it for
every pass of a linkage.

## Choose phonetic keys by how much they merge

Every phonetic code merges some spellings and separates others, and the
trade-off is block size against recall. Comparing codes on the name
variants you actually expect shows the differences quickly:

```{r}
#| label: phonetic-keys
surn <- c("SMITH", "SMYTH", "SCHMIDT", "MEYER", "MEIER", "MCDONALD",
          "MACDONALD", "THOMPSON", "TOMSON", "NGUYEN", "NGYUEN", "PHILLIPS",
          "FILLIPS", "O'BRIEN", "OBRIEN", "BRIEN")
codes <- data.frame(name = surn, soundex = soundex(surn), nysiis = nysiis(surn),
                    metaphone = metaphone(surn), statcan = statcan(surn),
                    phonex = phonex(surn), onca = onca(surn),
                    caverphone = caverphone(surn))
codes
sapply(codes[-1], function(k) length(unique(k)))   # fewer = coarser blocks
```

Soundex merges `SCHMIDT` with `SMITH` but separates `PHILLIPS` from
`FILLIPS`; Phonex and ONCA join the latter pair. NYSIIS and Metaphone
separate more spellings, which makes smaller blocks and needs more passes.
Caverphone was designed for New Zealand and Australian electoral-roll
names.

The same comparison on your own file, rather than on a list of variants,
says how big the blocks will be:

```{r}
#| label: phonetic-block-sizes
sizes <- sapply(list(exact = enrol$surname, soundex = soundex(enrol$surname),
                     nysiis = nysiis(enrol$surname), phonex = phonex(enrol$surname),
                     dmetaphone = double_metaphone(enrol$surname)$primary),
                function(k) c(blocks = length(unique(k)),
                              largest = max(tabulate(match(k, unique(k)))),
                              pairs_per_1k = round(sum(tabulate(match(k, unique(k)))^2) /
                                                   length(k) / 1000, 1)))
sizes
```

`pairs_per_1k` is the number of candidate pairs, in thousands, that the key
alone would generate against a file of the same size -- the number that
decides whether a pass is affordable.

Names from more than one language tradition need more than one code.
`daitch_mokotoff()` returns up to several codes per name, so a name with
an ambiguous pronunciation lands in every block it might belong to:

```{r}
#| label: dmsoundex
daitch_mokotoff(c("SCHWARZ", "SHVARTZ", "MOSKOWITZ", "MOSKOVITZ"))
```

The Match Rating Approach is designed as a comparison rather than a key:
`mra_compare()` says whether two names match under its rules.

```{r}
#| label: mra
mra_compare(c("SMITH", "BYRNE", "CATHERINE"), c("SMYTH", "BOERN", "KATHRYN"))
```

## Candidates without blocking keys

When there is no good key, search for similar strings directly; none of
these functions builds the full comparison matrix.

`fuzzy_within()` returns every table entry within `k` edits of each query,
using SymSpell's symmetric-delete index -- the right tool for checking
typed values against a reference list such as a street or suburb
gazetteer:

```{r}
#| label: fuzzy-within
gazetteer <- sort(unique(enrol$suburb))
typed <- c("RICHMOND", "FITZROI", "ST KILDAA", "CAMBERWEL", "NOWHERE")
w <- fuzzy_within(typed, gazetteer, max_distance = 2)
data.frame(typed = typed[w$query_index], suburb = gazetteer[w$table_index],
           distance = w$distance)
```

Results come ordered by distance, so the first row per query is the best,
and `NOWHERE` returns nothing rather than a wrong answer. The result is
exact -- the same pairs as filtering a full `osa_distance_matrix()` -- at a
fraction of the cost for large tables.

For names that differ by whole words -- an organisation with and without
`THE`, `UNI` for `UNIVERSITY`, an extra department -- edit distance is the
wrong measure. `tfidf_match()` compares TF-IDF-weighted character n-grams,
so rare, informative words dominate and common ones barely count:

```{r}
#| label: tfidf
orgs <- c("UNIVERSITY OF QUEENSLAND", "QUEENSLAND UNIVERSITY OF TECHNOLOGY",
          "GRIFFITH UNIVERSITY", "QUEENSLAND HEALTH", "BRISBANE CITY COUNCIL",
          "LOGAN CITY COUNCIL", "UNIVERSITY OF SYDNEY")
qs <- c("THE UNIVERSITY OF QUEENSLAND", "QLD UNIVERSITY OF TECHNOLOGY",
        "BRISBANE CITY COUNCIL LIBRARIES", "GRIFFITH UNI", "SYDNEY UNIVERSITY")
data.frame(query = qs, match = orgs[tfidf_match(qs, orgs)])
tfidf_top_n("QLD UNIVERSITY OF TECHNOLOGY", orgs, top_n = 3)
```

For long text -- product descriptions, case notes, addresses with
free-text additions -- `minhash_pairs()` finds pairs whose q-gram sets
probably overlap by at least `threshold` (Jaccard), using
locality-sensitive hashing, and verifies each candidate exactly.

```{r}
#| label: minhash
notes <- c("Unit 4, 9 King St Brisbane - deliver to rear entrance",
           "U4 9 King Street, Brisbane (rear entrance delivery)",
           "12 Logan Road Woolloongabba, upstairs office",
           "12 Logan Rd, Woolloongabba - upstairs office suite",
           "88 Gympie Road Chermside")
minhash_pairs(notes, threshold = 0.4)
```

## Score with the comparison that fits the field

Jaro-Winkler is the standard for short names, but each kind of field has
its own kind of difference. @sec-uc-metrics measures every comparator in
the package against labelled name and address pairs and says which to
reach for when; the short version is below.

**Phonetic misspellings** (`PH`/`F`, `C`/`K`) cost less under `editex()`,
an edit distance whose substitution cost depends on whether the letters
sound alike:

```{r}
#| label: editex
a <- c("PHILIP", "CATHERINE", "SHEPHERD", "STEPHEN")
b <- c("FILIP", "KATHRYN", "SHEPPARD", "STEVEN")
data.frame(a, b, levenshtein = round(levenshtein_similarity(a, b), 3),
           editex = round(editex_similarity(a, b), 3))
```

**Multi-word names** with reordered, missing or extra words suit
`monge_elkan()` (the mean best match of each word) or
`jaro_winkler_tokens()`. This is the comparison to use on a name field
that was never split:

```{r}
#| label: monge-elkan
a <- c("JOHN PAUL SMITH", "MARY JANE O BRIEN", "ROBERT JONES", "LI WEI CHEN")
b <- c("SMITH JOHN", "OBRIEN MARY", "BOB JONES", "CHEN LI WEI")
data.frame(a, b,
           jaro_winkler = round(jaro_winkler(a, b), 3),
           monge_elkan  = round(monge_elkan(a, b), 3),
           tokens       = round(jaro_winkler_tokens(a, b), 3))
```

Plain Jaro-Winkler is the wrong tool on every row here. `monge_elkan()`
holds up best when a word is *missing* (`JOHN PAUL SMITH` against
`SMITH JOHN`) or replaced by a nickname (`ROBERT` / `BOB`), because it
scores each word against its own best partner and averages;
`jaro_winkler_tokens()` is the stronger of the two on a clean reordering,
and it also folds punctuation and spacing, which is what rescues
`O BRIEN` / `OBRIEN`. Neither recovers a name whose words were both
reordered *and* split differently --- row 2 --- which is the case for
comparing the parsed `surname` and `given_name` fields separately instead.

**One string inside another** -- a street address inside a full address
line -- is local alignment: `smith_waterman()` scores the best-matching
substring, and `lcs_str()` returns the longest common substring:

```{r}
#| label: smith-waterman
smith_waterman(c("9 KING ST", "9 KING ST"),
               c("UNIT 4 9 KING ST BRISBANE", "19 KINGS ST"))
lcs_str("9 KING ST", "UNIT 4 9 KING ST BRISBANE")
```

**A date of birth** is not a string: compare the day numbers, so that
2 January and 1 January are one apart rather than two characters apart.

```{r}
#| label: dob-compare
d1 <- as.Date(c("1985-03-14", "1985-03-05", "1985-03-15", "1985-03-15"))
d2 <- as.Date(c("1985-03-15", "1985-05-03", "1986-03-15", "1985-03-15"))
# date_parts() splits both sides in one pass, which is cheaper than
# formatting them and much cheaper than three format() calls each.
pa <- date_parts(d1)
pb <- date_parts(d2)
data.frame(d1, d2,
           days_apart = abs(as.numeric(d1 - d2)),
           transposed = pa$year == pb$year & pa$day == pb$month &
                        pa$month == pb$day & pa$day != pa$month,
           same_year_month = pa$year == pb$year & pa$month == pb$month)
```

When a pair goes to clerical review, `edit_ops()` explains a distance as
the edits themselves:

```{r}
#| label: edit-ops
edit_ops("JONATHAN", "JONHATAN", type = "opcodes")
```

## From matched pairs to entities

Deduplication needs one identifier per entity, not a list of pairs.
`cluster_pairs()` joins records connected by any chain of matches:

```{r}
#| label: cluster-pairs
# 1 matches 2, 2 matches 3, 4 matches 5; record 6 matches nothing
cluster_pairs(c(1, 2, 4), c(2, 3, 5), n = 6)
```

It takes the pair table directly, so the usual last line of a
deduplication is one call. On the stacked extract above:

```{r}
#| label: cluster-from-pairs
accepted <- dup[dup$given > 0.85 & dup$surname > 0.85, ]
entity <- cluster_pairs(accepted, n = nrow(combined))
c(records = length(entity), entities = max(entity),
  merged = length(entity) - max(entity))
table(cluster_size = tabulate(entity))
```

Chaining is the risk, and it is visible right there. The stacked extract
holds each shared person exactly twice, so a perfect deduplication would
leave clusters of size 1 and 2 only. The clusters of eight and thirteen
are not people recorded thirteen times; they are chains, where A matched
B, B matched C, and nothing ever compared A with C. Three defences, in
order of how much work they are:

- resolve the pairs one-to-one before clustering, keeping each record's
  single best partner (@sec-workflow does this);
- raise the threshold for a pair that would join two already-large
  clusters;
- review the largest clusters by hand. There are few of them, and they are
  where the wrong merges live.

A cluster is only as sound as its weakest accepted pair, so it is the
*minimum* pair score inside a large cluster that is worth looking at, not
the average.

## At scale

The whole of the linkage above -- four blocking passes and seven
comparators over 20,000 enrolment records and 15,000 claims -- is one
`rLink()` call. The same call on ten times the data:

```{r}
#| label: scale
big <- people_files(n_enrol = 200000, overlap = 0.6)
big_claims <- big$claims
nm <- fsquish(fupper(big_claims$patient_name))
rs <- fsquish(freplace_tokens(ftrimws(fsplit_field(nm, ",", 2)),
                              titles, rep("", length(titles))))
big_std <- data.frame(
    given_name = fsplit_field(rs, " ", 1),
    surname    = ftrimws(fsplit_field(nm, ",", 1)),
    dob        = fas.Date(big_claims$date_of_birth, format = "dmy"),
    postcode   = fpad(as.character(big_claims$postcode), 4, pad = "0"),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
big_enrol <- big$enrol

system.time(
    out <- rLink(big_enrol, big_std,
        block = list(list(soundex(surname), dob),
                     list(soundex(given_name), dob),
                     list(soundex(surname), fsubstr(given_name, 1, 1), postcode)),
        compare = list(surname = jaro_winkler(surname),
                       given   = jaro_winkler_tokens(given_name),
                       dob     = (function(a, b) a == b)(dob)),
        keep = character())
)
c(records_a = nrow(big_enrol), records_b = nrow(big_std),
  pairs_possible = as.numeric(nrow(big_enrol)) * nrow(big_std),
  pairs_compared = nrow(out),
  blocking_recall = round(sum(same_person(big, out$index_1, out$index_2)) /
                          true_pair_count(big), 4))
```

`keep = character()` carries none of the input columns onto the output,
which is what you want once the pipeline is no longer being read by eye:
the indices and the scores are enough to join back.
